concepts.def: The diffusion of gases across a surface between an organism and its environment: oxygen is taken up and carbon dioxide released by aerobic organisms, and the reverse by photosynthesizing tissue in the light. It is a vital function in all organisms, from unicellular organisms exchanging gases across the plasma membrane to large animals and plants with specialized exchange surfaces.

The surface area of an organism or cell divided by its volume. As size increases, volume grows faster than surface area, so the ratio decreases: a cube of side 1 mm has a ratio of 6 mm⁻¹, a cube of side 2 mm a ratio of 3 mm⁻¹. A smaller ratio means less exchange surface is available to supply each unit of respiring volume, which is why larger organisms need specialized gas-exchange systems.

The distance a gas must diffuse between the exterior of an organism and the cells that use or produce it. Because the time taken for diffusion rises steeply with distance, gas exchange by diffusion alone is only adequate for small organisms; in a large organism the distance from the centre to the exterior is too great, so gases must be carried by a transport system to and from a specialized exchange surface.

A surface across which gases diffuse between an organism and its environment, such as the alveolar surface of a lung or the mesophyll cell surfaces bordering the air spaces of a leaf. Effective exchange surfaces are permeable to the gases, consist of a thin tissue layer so that the diffusion distance is short, are moist so that gases dissolve before crossing membranes, and have a large surface area so that much gas can cross at once.

The property of a membrane or tissue layer that allows a substance to pass through it. A gas-exchange surface must be permeable to oxygen and carbon dioxide; both are small, non-polar molecules that pass freely through the phospholipid bilayer of the cells forming the surface, whereas a layer such as the waxy cuticle of a leaf is almost impermeable to them.

A difference in concentration of a substance between two regions. Net diffusion of oxygen across an exchange surface continues only while its concentration is higher on the outside than in the blood; if exchange were allowed to reach equilibrium, net diffusion would stop. Animals maintain the gradient by supplying fresh air or water to the outer side (ventilation) and by carrying blood continuously past the inner side through dense networks of blood vessels, so that oxygenated blood is replaced by deoxygenated blood.

The movement of the external medium across a gas-exchange surface so that the gas concentrations next to the surface stay close to those of the environment. Lungs are ventilated with air, which is drawn in and expelled; gills are ventilated with water, which is passed over the gill surfaces. Ventilation is distinct from gas exchange itself, which is the diffusion of gases across the surface.

One of the millions of tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles in a mammalian lung, where gas exchange takes place. Each alveolus has a wall one cell thick, lined with a film of moisture and surrounded by an extensive capillary bed, so the diffusion distance between air and blood is very short. Together the alveoli provide a very large surface area for gas exchange.

A phospholipid-rich secretion from cells of the alveolar wall that forms a layer on the moist inner surface of the alveoli. It reduces the surface tension of the water film, which would otherwise tend to pull the walls of each small alveolus inward; this prevents the alveoli collapsing and allows them to expand easily during inspiration.

One of the narrow airways formed by repeated branching of the bronchi within a mammalian lung. The branched network of bronchioles carries air to and from the alveoli at its ends; the branching allows a very large number of alveoli, and therefore a very large exchange surface, to be packed into the volume of the thorax. Gas exchange takes place across the alveolar walls, not the walls of the bronchioles.

A sheet of muscle separating the thorax from the abdomen. When it contracts it flattens, increasing the volume of the thorax; when it relaxes it returns to a dome shape, decreasing the volume. In inspiration its contraction lowers the pressure in the lungs below atmospheric pressure so air flows in.

Two layers of muscle between the ribs that act antagonistically. Contraction of the external intercostal muscles moves the ribs upward and outward, increasing the volume of the thorax during inspiration; contraction of the internal intercostal muscles moves the ribs downward and inward, decreasing the volume during forced expiration.

The muscles of the abdominal wall, which contract during forced expiration. Their contraction raises the pressure in the abdomen and pushes the abdominal organs up against the relaxed diaphragm, so the diaphragm domes further into the thorax and the volume of the thorax decreases. They are relaxed during inspiration, when the contracting diaphragm pushes the abdominal organs downward.

The cycle of inspiration and expiration that moves air into and out of the alveoli. Inspiration is active: the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, the ribs rise, the thorax volume increases, pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure and air flows in. Quiet expiration is largely passive, driven by relaxation of these muscles and elastic recoil of the lungs; forced expiration uses contraction of the internal intercostal and abdominal muscles to reduce the thorax volume further. The lungs contain no skeletal muscle and cannot move air themselves.
The volume of air moved into or out of the lungs in one breath during normal, relaxed breathing; typically about 0.5 dm³ in an adult at rest. It increases during exercise as breaths become deeper.

The maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after the deepest possible inhalation. It is the sum of the tidal volume, the inspiratory reserve volume and the expiratory reserve volume, and is typically 3 to 5 dm³ in an adult. It is not the total volume of the lungs, because some air always remains in the lungs after a maximal exhalation.

The additional volume of air that can be inhaled after a normal tidal inhalation, measured from the top of a resting breath to the peak of the deepest possible inhalation. It does not include the tidal volume.

The additional volume of air that can be exhaled after a normal tidal exhalation, measured from the bottom of a resting breath to the end of the deepest possible exhalation. It does not include the tidal volume.

An instrument that records the volume of air breathed in and out through a mouthpiece, producing a trace of lung volume against time. Tidal volume is read from the height of a resting breath, the reserve volumes from the extra movements above and below it when the subject inhales and exhales maximally, and vital capacity from the full excursion from deepest inhalation to deepest exhalation. Simpler measurements can be made by exhaling into a bag or through a tube into an inverted, water-filled container.

A layer of wax secreted by the epidermal cells onto the outer surface of a leaf. It is impermeable to water and almost impermeable to gases, so it reduces water loss from the leaf surface; gases enter and leave the leaf through the stomata rather than across the cuticle.

The single layer of closely packed cells covering the upper and lower surfaces of a leaf. It protects the tissues inside, secretes the waxy cuticle and, in most dicotyledonous leaves, contains most of the stomata on its lower surface. Its cells are usually transparent and lack chloroplasts, apart from the guard cells.

The layer of loosely packed, irregularly shaped photosynthetic cells in the lower part of a leaf, separated by interconnected air spaces that open to the stomata. The moist surfaces of the mesophyll cells bordering the air spaces form the gas-exchange surface of the leaf: carbon dioxide dissolves and diffuses into the cells and oxygen diffuses out. The air spaces give the leaf a very large internal surface area and let gases reach the palisade cells above.

A stoma is a pore in the epidermis, bordered by a pair of guard cells, through which gases diffuse between the air spaces of the leaf and the atmosphere. The guard cells regulate the aperture: when they take up water and become turgid, their unevenly thickened walls make them curve apart and the pore opens; when they lose water and become flaccid, the pore closes. This allows the leaf to balance carbon dioxide uptake against water loss.

A vascular bundle running through the mesophyll of a leaf, containing xylem and phloem. Xylem delivers water to the leaf, replacing the water lost by transpiration and keeping the mesophyll cell surfaces moist so that gases can dissolve; phloem carries away the sugars made in photosynthesis. Veins do not carry gases: oxygen and carbon dioxide move through the leaf by diffusion.

A drawing that shows the outline and relative position of each tissue in a section, without drawing individual cells. A plan diagram of a transverse section of a dicotyledonous leaf shows, from the upper surface downward, the upper epidermis, the palisade mesophyll, the spongy mesophyll and the lower epidermis, with veins (vascular bundles) within the mesophyll; in a vein the xylem lies toward the upper surface and the phloem toward the lower surface.

The layer of closely packed, elongated cells, rich in chloroplasts, lying directly beneath the upper epidermis of a dicotyledonous leaf. It is the main photosynthetic tissue; its cells are positioned to absorb light entering through the transparent upper epidermis and obtain carbon dioxide from the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll below.

The loss of water vapour from the leaves and other aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata. It is a consequence of gas exchange: stomata must be open for carbon dioxide to diffuse in for photosynthesis, and while they are open water vapour, evaporated from the moist surfaces of the mesophyll cells into the air spaces, diffuses out down its concentration gradient to the drier atmosphere.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the rate of transpiration
concepts.def: Temperature, humidity, wind and light intensity. Higher temperature increases the rate by increasing evaporation and the water-vapour concentration inside the leaf; higher humidity decreases the rate by reducing the concentration gradient between the air spaces and the atmosphere; wind increases the rate by removing the layer of humid air at the leaf surface; higher light intensity increases the rate because it causes the stomata to open.

The number of stomata per unit area of leaf surface, usually expressed per mm². It is determined by counting the stomata visible in a field of view of known area, under a microscope at high power, and dividing the count by that area; counts from several fields of view are averaged before dividing.

An impression of a leaf surface made by painting the surface with clear nail varnish or similar material, allowing it to dry, and peeling it off with adhesive tape. Mounted on a slide, the cast shows the outlines of the epidermal cells and stomata and can be used, like a micrograph of the epidermis, to count stomata and determine stomatal density.

Repeated measurements of the same quantity, such as counts of stomata in several different fields of view on the same leaf. Biological material is variable, so single counts differ from place to place; taking replicates reveals this variability and allows a mean to be calculated, which increases the reliability of the quantitative data.

The oxygen-transporting protein of red blood cells, consisting of four polypeptide subunits each carrying a haem group with an iron ion that can bind one oxygen molecule. One haemoglobin molecule can therefore carry up to four oxygen molecules; it loads oxygen where the oxygen concentration is high, in the lungs, and unloads it where the concentration is low, in respiring tissues.

The property of haemoglobin by which binding of an oxygen molecule to one haem group changes the conformation of the whole protein, increasing the affinity of the remaining haem groups for oxygen. Binding of the first oxygen is therefore the hardest and each subsequent oxygen binds more readily; the reverse occurs during unloading. Cooperative binding explains the S-shaped oxygen dissociation curve.

Binding of carbon dioxide to haemoglobin at sites other than the oxygen-binding haem groups, on the polypeptide chains. This binding changes the conformation of the protein and lowers its affinity for oxygen, promoting the release of oxygen in tissues where carbon dioxide concentration is high; carbon dioxide does not compete with oxygen for the haem groups.

The form of haemoglobin in the red blood cells of a foetus, which has different polypeptide subunits from adult haemoglobin and a higher affinity for oxygen. At the oxygen concentration in the placenta, where maternal haemoglobin is releasing oxygen, foetal haemoglobin loads oxygen to a higher saturation, so oxygen passes from maternal blood to foetal blood; its dissociation curve lies to the left of the adult curve.

The decrease in the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen caused by an increase in carbon dioxide concentration, seen as a shift of the oxygen dissociation curve to the right. Carbon dioxide binds allosterically to haemoglobin and, by forming carbonic acid, lowers the pH of the blood; both effects change the protein's conformation so that more oxygen dissociates at any given oxygen concentration. Actively respiring tissues produce more carbon dioxide and therefore receive more oxygen from the blood that passes through them.

A graph of the percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen against the oxygen concentration (partial pressure of oxygen) of the surroundings. The curve is S-shaped because of cooperative binding: at low oxygen concentration saturation rises slowly, then steeply once the first oxygen molecules bound have raised the affinity of the remaining haem groups, and finally it levels off as the haem groups approach full occupancy. The steep region corresponds to the oxygen concentrations found in respiring tissues, so a small fall in concentration there causes a large release of oxygen.

The readiness with which haemoglobin binds and retains oxygen, shown by the position of its dissociation curve. A curve further to the left indicates higher affinity, because haemoglobin reaches a given saturation at a lower oxygen concentration; a curve further to the right indicates lower affinity, so more oxygen is released at a given oxygen concentration.

mcqs.q: Why does gas exchange become a greater challenge as organisms increase in size?
options: The surface area-to-volume ratio decreases, and the distance from the centre of the organism to its exterior increases.
The surface area-to-volume ratio increases, so far more gas has to cross each unit of the exchange surface.
Only animals with lungs or gills exchange gases, so the challenge arises once an organism is big enough to have them.
A large organism uses more oxygen in total; the distance gases must diffuse to reach its cells makes no difference.
mcqs.specStatementText: Gas exchange gets harder as organisms get bigger
mcqs.explain: Volume grows faster than surface area, so a large organism has proportionally less surface across which to exchange gases, and its inner cells are too far from the surface for diffusion alone to supply them. Both effects make specialized gas-exchange surfaces and transport systems necessary.
rationales: Volume grows faster than surface area, so a large organism has proportionally less surface across which to exchange gases, and its inner cells are too far from the surface for diffusion alone to supply them. Both effects make specialized gas-exchange surfaces and transport systems necessary.

A student who reasons that a bigger organism has 'more surface' picks this. Total surface area does increase, but the ratio of surface to volume decreases, so there is less surface per unit of respiring tissue, not more.

A student who equates gas exchange with breathing picks this. Gas exchange is a vital function in all organisms, including unicellular organisms and plants; the challenge grows with size because the surface area-to-volume ratio falls and the diffusion distance rises, not because small organisms do not exchange gases.

A student who thinks diffusion is fast over any distance picks this. Diffusion time rises steeply with distance, and the distance from centre to exterior grows with size, so distance is one of the two reasons the challenge increases.

mcqs.q: Three cubes are used to model organisms of different sizes. Their surface area-to-volume ratios are: side 1 mm, 6 mm⁻¹; side 2 mm, 3 mm⁻¹; side 4 mm, 1.5 mm⁻¹. Which conclusion is supported by these values?
options: The largest cube has the most surface per unit of volume, because its total surface area is the greatest.
Each doubling of the side halves the ratio, leaving proportionally less surface to supply each unit of volume.
The ratio should have stayed constant as the cubes were scaled up, so the values must contain a measurement error.
Only the fall in the ratio matters; the distance from the centre to the surface has no effect on diffusion.
mcqs.specStatementText: Gas exchange gets harder as organisms get bigger
mcqs.explain: From 6 to 3 to 1.5 mm⁻¹, the ratio halves each time the side doubles, because surface area rises fourfold while volume rises eightfold. A larger organism therefore has less exchange surface for each unit of respiring tissue, which is why gas exchange becomes more challenging with size.
rationales: A student who confuses total surface area with the ratio picks this. The 4 mm cube does have the largest total area, but the data show it has the least surface per unit volume: 1.5 mm⁻¹ against 6 mm⁻¹ for the smallest cube.

From 6 to 3 to 1.5 mm⁻¹, the ratio halves each time the side doubles, because surface area rises fourfold while volume rises eightfold. A larger organism therefore has less exchange surface for each unit of respiring tissue, which is why gas exchange becomes more challenging with size.

A student who thinks area and volume scale by the same factor picks this. Area scales with length squared and volume with length cubed, so the ratio must fall; the values are exactly what the geometry predicts.

A student who believes diffusion is equally fast over any distance picks this. The larger cube's centre is further from its surface, and diffusion time rises steeply with distance, so distance is a second, independent reason larger organisms need transport systems.

mcqs.q: Why is the surface of a gas-exchange organ kept moist?
options: The moisture is not needed for exchange; it only keeps the cells of the surface from drying out and dying.
The moisture forms a sticky layer that traps dust and pathogens before they reach the exchange surface.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolve in the film of water before diffusing across the cell membranes.
The water is absorbed into the blood across the surface, carrying the dissolved oxygen in with it.
mcqs.specStatementText: What a good exchange surface looks like
mcqs.explain: Gases cross plasma membranes only in solution. The thin film of moisture lets oxygen dissolve and then diffuse into the cells and blood, and lets carbon dioxide dissolve and diffuse out; moisture is therefore a property of every gas-exchange surface.
rationales: A student who pictures gases crossing the surface as gases picks this. Keeping cells alive is a benefit, but the moisture is essential to exchange itself: gases can only cross the plasma membranes in solution.

A student who confuses the moist film with the mucus of the airways picks this. Trapping particles is the job of mucus in the trachea and bronchi; the film on the exchange surface is there so that gases can dissolve.

Gases cross plasma membranes only in solution. The thin film of moisture lets oxygen dissolve and then diffuse into the cells and blood, and lets carbon dioxide dissolve and diffuse out; moisture is therefore a property of every gas-exchange surface.

A student who pictures oxygen being taken in with water picks this. The film of water stays on the surface; only the dissolved oxygen diffuses across the membranes, down its concentration gradient, into the blood.

mcqs.q: A fish rests in still, well-oxygenated water. What keeps the oxygen concentration gradient across its gill surface steep?
options: The water around the gills contains dissolved oxygen, so the gradient is maintained by the water itself.
Once oxygen has diffused into the blood the gradient is fixed and does not need to be maintained further.
Blood is held in the gill capillaries until it is saturated, so that every red blood cell loads fully.
Water is pumped over the gills while blood flows continuously through their dense capillaries.
mcqs.explain: Ventilation with water keeps the outer side of the gill surface rich in oxygen, and continuous blood flow through the dense network of capillaries keeps the inner side low in oxygen by carrying oxygenated blood away. Together they maintain the concentration gradient.
rationales: A student who thinks gills need no ventilation picks this. The layer of water in contact with the gill surface is depleted of oxygen within moments, and diffusion through still water is very slow, so the fish must pump fresh water over the gills.
A student who believes a gradient looks after itself picks this. Diffusion destroys the gradient that drives it, so it must be continuously renewed by ventilation and blood flow.

A student who thinks blood loads more if it lingers picks this. Blood that stays approaches equilibrium with the water and net diffusion stops; continuous flow replaces it with deoxygenated blood, keeping the gradient steep.

Ventilation with water keeps the outer side of the gill surface rich in oxygen, and continuous blood flow through the dense network of capillaries keeps the inner side low in oxygen by carrying oxygenated blood away. Together they maintain the concentration gradient.

mcqs.q: Suppose that blood flow through the gill capillaries of an anaesthetized fish is stopped while water continues to flow over the gills, and that oxygen uptake across the gills falls almost to zero within a minute. Which explanation is best supported?
options: With no blood flow, oxygen built up in the stationary blood until its concentration matched the water's, so the gradient was lost.
Stopping blood flow cannot affect the gradient across the gill; the water flowing over the gills must have run out of oxygen.
Blood held still in the capillaries should load more fully, so the fall must have been caused by damage to the gill surface.
Oxygen enters with water absorbed into the blood, and once the blood stopped moving no more water could be taken up.
mcqs.explain: This is the correct explanation. Once the blood in the capillaries was as rich in oxygen as the water, there was no concentration gradient and net diffusion stopped; continuous blood flow normally removes oxygenated blood and keeps the gradient steep.
rationales: This is the correct explanation. Once the blood in the capillaries was as rich in oxygen as the water, there was no concentration gradient and net diffusion stopped; continuous blood flow normally removes oxygenated blood and keeps the gradient steep.

A student who thinks the gradient is fixed once established picks this. Fresh water continued to flow, so the outer side of the gradient was maintained; it was the inner side, the blood, that came to equilibrium when flow stopped.

A student who believes stationary blood absorbs more picks this. Stationary blood equilibrates within seconds and then absorbs nothing; the result is exactly what continuous flow normally prevents, not evidence of damage.

A student who pictures oxygen entering dissolved in absorbed water picks this. Water is not absorbed at the gill; dissolved oxygen diffuses across the membranes on its own, and it stopped because the gradient was lost.

mcqs.q: What is the function of surfactant in the alveoli of a mammalian lung?
options: It traps dust and microorganisms in a sticky layer so that they can be swept out of the lungs.
It lowers the surface tension of the moisture lining the alveoli, so they do not collapse and inflate easily.
It is the film of water absorbed into the blood, carrying the oxygen dissolved in it across the alveolar wall.
It dries the alveolar lining so that gases cross the wall as gases rather than having to dissolve first.
mcqs.explain: Water has a high surface tension that would pull the walls of each tiny alveolus inward and collapse it. Surfactant, secreted onto the moist lining, reduces this surface tension so the alveoli stay open and expand with little effort during inspiration.
rationales: A student who assumes every airway secretion is mucus picks this. Trapping particles is the role of mucus in the trachea and bronchi; surfactant is a phospholipid layer with a physical role at the alveolar surface.

Water has a high surface tension that would pull the walls of each tiny alveolus inward and collapse it. Surfactant, secreted onto the moist lining, reduces this surface tension so the alveoli stay open and expand with little effort during inspiration.

A student who pictures oxygen entering with absorbed water picks this. The moist film stays on the alveolar surface and only the dissolved oxygen diffuses across; surfactant is a phospholipid layer on that film that lowers its surface tension.

A student who thinks moisture hinders gas exchange picks this. The lining must stay moist because gases cross membranes only in solution; surfactant reduces the surface tension of that moisture rather than removing it.

mcqs.q: Mammalian lungs contain a branched network of bronchioles ending in millions of alveoli. How does this branching contribute to gas exchange?
options: It multiplies the area of airway wall across which gases are exchanged into the blood as air travels inward.
It lets the lungs grow larger, and a larger organ must have a bigger surface for gas exchange.
It packs a very large alveolar surface, each part close to a capillary bed, into the volume of the thorax.
It houses the muscle that contracts to pump air in and out of the alveoli found at the end of every branch.
mcqs.explain: Repeated branching ends in millions of alveoli, each thin-walled and wrapped in capillaries. The combined alveolar surface of tens of square metres is fitted into a chest cavity of a few litres, giving the high surface area that gas exchange needs.
rationales: A student who thinks the whole airway tree exchanges gases picks this. Bronchiole walls are too thick and too far from capillaries for exchange; the branching matters because of the number of alveoli it delivers air to.

A student who equates size with surface area picks this. Enlarging an organ raises its volume faster than its surface; the large area comes from subdivision into millions of alveoli, not from the lungs being big.

Repeated branching ends in millions of alveoli, each thin-walled and wrapped in capillaries. The combined alveolar surface of tens of square metres is fitted into a chest cavity of a few litres, giving the high surface area that gas exchange needs.

A student who thinks the lungs move air by their own muscle picks this. Air is moved by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles changing the volume of the thorax; the bronchioles conduct air, they do not pump it.

mcqs.q: Which sequence of events draws air into the lungs during inspiration?
options: Air entering the lungs inflates them, and the inflating lungs push the ribs outward and the diaphragm downward.
The muscular walls of the lungs contract, widening the alveoli and sucking air in through the trachea.
The diaphragm relaxes and rises into a dome, and the ribs move up so that air is drawn in to fill the space.
The diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thorax volume rises and lung pressure falls.
mcqs.explain: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles increases the volume of the thorax. The pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, and air flows in down the pressure gradient.
rationales: A student who reverses cause and effect, as in the balloon model, picks this. The ribs and diaphragm move first, lowering the pressure in the lungs; air flows in because of that pressure difference.

A student who thinks the lungs are muscular picks this. Lungs contain no skeletal muscle; the thorax is enlarged by the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles, and the lungs expand passively with it.

A student who pictures the diaphragm's dome as its active state picks this. A relaxed, domed diaphragm reduces thorax volume and belongs to expiration; in inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens.

Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles increases the volume of the thorax. The pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, and air flows in down the pressure gradient.

mcqs.q: A person breathes out as hard as possible. What is the role of the abdominal muscles in this forced expiration?
options: They contract, pushing the abdominal organs up against the relaxed diaphragm so that the volume of the thorax decreases.
They relax so that the diaphragm can rise passively, and so they have no active role in forcing the air out.
They contract together with the diaphragm, which pushes upward to squeeze the air out of the lungs from below.
They have no role, because the lungs themselves contract to expel the air once the person decides to breathe out.
mcqs.explain: Contraction of the abdominal muscles raises the pressure in the abdomen and forces the organs upward against the diaphragm, which has relaxed into its dome. Together with the internal intercostal muscles pulling the ribs down and in, this reduces the thorax volume and expels air.
rationales: Contraction of the abdominal muscles raises the pressure in the abdomen and forces the organs upward against the diaphragm, which has relaxed into its dome. Together with the internal intercostal muscles pulling the ribs down and in, this reduces the thorax volume and expels air.

A student who thinks the abdominal muscles work only during inspiration picks this. They are relaxed during inspiration; in forced expiration they contract, and it is their contraction that pushes the diaphragm upward.
A student who thinks the diaphragm contracts to push upward picks this. A muscle cannot push; the diaphragm relaxes in expiration and is moved up by the abdominal organs beneath it.
A student who believes the lungs are muscular picks this. The lungs cannot contract; forced expiration depends on the abdominal and internal intercostal muscles reducing the volume of the thorax.

mcqs.q: A student's spirometer readings are: tidal volume 0.5 dm³, inspiratory reserve volume 3.0 dm³, expiratory reserve volume 1.2 dm³. What is the student's vital capacity?
options: 4.2 dm³
4.7 dm³
3.5 dm³
1.7 dm³
mcqs.explain: Vital capacity is the maximum volume that can be exhaled after the deepest inhalation, which is tidal volume + inspiratory reserve + expiratory reserve = 0.5 + 3.0 + 1.2 = 4.7 dm³.
rationales: A student who thinks each reserve already includes the tidal volume adds only the two reserves: 3.0 + 1.2. The reserves are the extra volumes beyond a normal breath, so the tidal volume of 0.5 dm³ must be added as well.
Vital capacity is the maximum volume that can be exhaled after the deepest inhalation, which is tidal volume + inspiratory reserve + expiratory reserve = 0.5 + 3.0 + 1.2 = 4.7 dm³.

A student who takes vital capacity to be the deepest breath in from rest adds tidal volume and inspiratory reserve only: 0.5 + 3.0. The expiratory reserve of 1.2 dm³ can also be exhaled and is part of the vital capacity.

A student who measures only the exhalation after a normal breath in adds tidal volume and expiratory reserve: 0.5 + 1.2. Vital capacity must start from a maximal inhalation, so the inspiratory reserve of 3.0 dm³ is included.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly defines vital capacity?
options: The maximum volume that can be inhaled in one breath from the end of a normal exhalation.
The maximum volume that can be exhaled after a normal, resting inhalation.
The maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after the deepest possible inhalation.
The total volume of air in the lungs when they are inflated as fully as possible.
mcqs.explain: Vital capacity runs from the peak of a maximal inhalation to the end of a maximal exhalation, and equals tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve plus expiratory reserve. It is measured by inhaling fully and then exhaling fully into a spirometer.
rationales: A student who pictures 'capacity' as filling up from the resting position picks this. This is tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve; vital capacity also includes the expiratory reserve that can be forced out below a normal breath.

A student who focuses on the exhalation into the spirometer and forgets the maximal inhalation first picks this. This is tidal volume plus expiratory reserve, which leaves out the inspiratory reserve.

Vital capacity runs from the peak of a maximal inhalation to the end of a maximal exhalation, and equals tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve plus expiratory reserve. It is measured by inhaling fully and then exhaling fully into a spirometer.

A student who reads 'capacity' as the whole contents of the lungs picks this. The lungs cannot be emptied completely by exhaling, so the total lung volume is larger than the vital capacity that a spirometer can measure.

mcqs.q: Which adaptation of a leaf allows carbon dioxide to reach the photosynthesizing cells inside it?
options: The cuticle and epidermis are permeable to gases, so carbon dioxide diffuses in across the whole surface of the leaf.
The veins carry carbon dioxide into the leaf from the stem and roots and take the oxygen produced away.
The palisade mesophyll lies just beneath the upper epidermis, so its cells absorb the gas from the outside air.
Air spaces between the spongy mesophyll cells connect to the stomata, so the gas diffuses to every cell.
mcqs.specStatementText: How a leaf is adapted for gas exchange
mcqs.explain: Carbon dioxide enters through the stomata and diffuses through the interconnected air spaces of the spongy mesophyll, dissolving in the moist surfaces of the mesophyll cells, including the palisade cells above. The air spaces give the leaf a large internal exchange surface.
rationales: A student who treats the whole leaf surface as the exchange surface picks this. The waxy cuticle is almost impermeable and the epidermal cells are tightly packed, so gases enter only through the stomata.
A student who models plant veins on blood vessels picks this. Xylem delivers water and phloem removes sugars; gases are not transported in veins but move through the leaf by diffusion.

A student who assumes the photosynthetic cells must be the exchange surface picks this. Palisade cells are covered by the epidermis and cuticle; they receive carbon dioxide from the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll beneath them.

Carbon dioxide enters through the stomata and diffuses through the interconnected air spaces of the spongy mesophyll, dissolving in the moist surfaces of the mesophyll cells, including the palisade cells above. The air spaces give the leaf a large internal exchange surface.

mcqs.q: What causes a stoma to open?
options: The guard cells take up water and swell, and their unevenly thickened walls make them bend apart.
The guard cells contract like muscle cells, pulling the two edges of the pore apart from one another.
The guard cells lose water and shrink, leaving a gap between them through which the gases can pass.
The plant needs to lose water to pull the transpiration stream up the xylem, and that need triggers opening.
mcqs.specStatementText: How a leaf is adapted for gas exchange
mcqs.explain: When guard cells gain water they swell. Because the wall next to the pore is thicker than the outer wall, the swelling bends each cell outward, away from its partner, and the pore between them opens; loss of water reverses this and closes the stoma.
rationales: When guard cells gain water they swell. Because the wall next to the pore is thicker than the outer wall, the swelling bends each cell outward, away from its partner, and the pore between them opens; loss of water reverses this and closes the stoma.
A student who supplies a muscle mechanism for anything that opens and closes picks this. Plant cells have no contractile machinery; guard cells change shape through changes in turgor.
A student who reasons that smaller cells leave a bigger hole picks this. Loss of water makes the guard cells flaccid and closes the stoma; it is swelling that opens it.

A student who treats transpiration as the purpose of stomata picks this. Stomata open when guard cells become turgid, in response to light and water availability, so that carbon dioxide can enter; the water loss and the pull on the xylem are consequences of opening, not its cause.

mcqs.q: Which statement about a plan diagram of a transverse section of a dicotyledonous leaf is correct?
options: It shows a few representative cells of each tissue in outline, including their nuclei and chloroplasts.
It shows the outline and position of each tissue, with the palisade mesophyll directly beneath the upper epidermis.
It shows each vein with phloem above the xylem, because the phloem lies nearer to the upper surface.
It shows the spongy mesophyll directly beneath the upper epidermis, above the palisade mesophyll.
mcqs.explain: A plan diagram is a low-power drawing of tissue regions, not cells. From the upper surface down it shows upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll and lower epidermis, with veins in the mesophyll; the palisade layer lies immediately under the upper epidermis where light enters.
rationales: A student who assumes every microscope drawing shows cells picks this. Individual cells belong in a high-power drawing; a plan diagram shows each tissue as a labelled region bounded by lines.

A plan diagram is a low-power drawing of tissue regions, not cells. From the upper surface down it shows upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll and lower epidermis, with veins in the mesophyll; the palisade layer lies immediately under the upper epidermis where light enters.
A student who transfers the stem arrangement, phloem outside xylem, picks this. In a leaf vein the xylem lies toward the upper surface and the phloem toward the lower surface.
A student who has learnt the layers as a list without their positions picks this. The palisade mesophyll lies under the upper epidermis and the spongy mesophyll below it, above the lower epidermis.

mcqs.q: Why is transpiration described as a consequence of gas exchange rather than as a process the leaf carries out for its own sake?
options: The plant opens its stomata in order to lose water, because transpiration is needed to pull water up through the xylem.
Water vapour escapes across the cuticle and epidermis wherever gases are exchanged over the leaf surface.
Stomata must be open for carbon dioxide to enter, and water vapour inevitably diffuses out through the same pores.
Transpiration is evaporation that depends only on temperature, so it happens whether or not the stomata are open.
mcqs.explain: Photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide, which can only enter through open stomata. While they are open, water vapour from the saturated air spaces diffuses out down its concentration gradient to the drier atmosphere; the water loss is an unavoidable side effect of gas exchange.
rationales: A student who treats the transpiration stream as the purpose of stomata picks this. Stomata open to admit carbon dioxide; the pull on the xylem is a useful consequence of the water loss, not the reason the stomata open.
A student who thinks gases and water cross the whole leaf surface picks this. The waxy cuticle is almost impermeable; both gas exchange and nearly all water loss take place through the stomata.

Photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide, which can only enter through open stomata. While they are open, water vapour from the saturated air spaces diffuses out down its concentration gradient to the drier atmosphere; the water loss is an unavoidable side effect of gas exchange.

A student who applies the everyday model of evaporation picks this. Water evaporates inside the leaf and can only escape through open stomata, which is exactly why transpiration is tied to gas exchange.

mcqs.q: A potometer was used to estimate transpiration by a leafy shoot at 20 °C. Water uptake in still air was 0.8 cm³ per hour; with a fan blowing air across the leaves, 1.9 cm³ per hour; in still air with a clear plastic bag enclosing the shoot, 0.3 cm³ per hour. Which conclusion is supported by these results?
options: Moving air raised the rate because the fan warmed the leaves, and warmer leaves evaporate water faster.
The humid air inside the bag should have increased the rate, so the reading of 0.3 cm³ per hour must be a fault.
The shoot cut down its transpiration inside the bag because it no longer needed to pull water up the stem.
Moving air and low humidity both steepen the water-vapour gradient from the air spaces to the atmosphere.
mcqs.explain: The fan removed the layer of humid air at the leaf surface, and the bag did the opposite by trapping water vapour around the shoot. Both results are explained by the size of the water-vapour concentration gradient that drives diffusion out of the stomata.
rationales: A student who thinks wind acts only through temperature picks this. The temperature was held at 20 °C; moving air raised the rate by sweeping away the humid layer next to the leaves, steepening the water-vapour gradient.

A student who believes humidity increases transpiration picks this. The bag trapped water vapour, which reduced the concentration gradient between the air spaces and the surrounding air, so the rate fell as expected.

A student who treats transpiration as something the plant does on purpose picks this. Transpiration is passive diffusion of water vapour; the rate fell because the humid air in the bag reduced the gradient, not because the plant chose to reduce it.

The fan removed the layer of humid air at the leaf surface, and the bag did the opposite by trapping water vapour around the shoot. Both results are explained by the size of the water-vapour concentration gradient that drives diffusion out of the stomata.

mcqs.q: A student counts the stomata visible in five different fields of view on the lower epidermis of a leaf: 22, 26, 19, 27 and 21. The area of one field of view at high power is 0.20 mm². What is the stomatal density?
options: 115 per mm²
575 per mm²
110 per mm²
4.6 per mm²
mcqs.explain: The mean count is (22 + 26 + 19 + 27 + 21) ÷ 5 = 23 stomata per field. Dividing by the area of a field, 23 ÷ 0.20 mm², gives 115 stomata per mm².
rationales: The mean count is (22 + 26 + 19 + 27 + 21) ÷ 5 = 23 stomata per field. Dividing by the area of a field, 23 ÷ 0.20 mm², gives 115 stomata per mm².

A student who pools the counts and divides the total, 115, by the area of one field picks this. The 115 stomata were counted over five fields, so either the mean count (23) is divided by 0.20 mm², or the total by 1.0 mm².

A student who thinks one count is enough uses only the first field: 22 ÷ 0.20. The counts vary from 19 to 27 because the leaf is variable, which is why the replicates are averaged before the density is calculated.
A student who multiplies the mean count by the area, 23 × 0.20, picks this. Density is a number per unit area, so the count is divided by the area; 4.6 stomata per mm² is far below any real leaf.

mcqs.q: Three students estimated the stomatal density of leaves from the same plant. Student A counted one field of view at high power and reported 90 per mm². Student B counted ten different fields, obtained values between 60 and 130 per mm², and reported the mean, 95 per mm². Student C counted the same single field as A five times, getting 90 per mm² each time. Which evaluation of these results is best?
options: C's result is the most reliable, because repeating the count five times confirmed that no counting error had been made.
B's estimate is most reliable, because the spread shows the leaf varies and the mean averages it out.
B's method is the least reliable, because results that vary from 60 to 130 show that the counting was inconsistent.
A would have been more reliable using low power, because one larger field of view contains more stomata.
mcqs.explain: Biological material is variable, so counts from different fields differ. Replicate counts in different fields reveal that variability and their mean is a more reliable estimate than any single field, however carefully or repeatedly it is counted.
rationales: A student who sees repetition only as a check for mistakes picks this. Recounting the same field confirms the count of that field, but it samples only one region and says nothing about how the density varies across the leaf.

Biological material is variable, so counts from different fields differ. Replicate counts in different fields reveal that variability and their mean is a more reliable estimate than any single field, however carefully or repeatedly it is counted.

A student who expects good replicates to be identical picks this. The spread reflects real variation in the leaf, not poor counting; it is exactly the variability that replicate fields are meant to capture and average.

A student who applies 'bigger sample is better' to a single field picks this. Stomata are counted at high power because they can be resolved reliably there; reliability comes from several independent fields, not from one bigger one.

mcqs.q: What is meant by cooperative binding of oxygen to haemoglobin?
options: Each of the four haem groups binds oxygen independently, with the same affinity whether or not the others are occupied.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide share the haem groups, taking turns to bind as their concentrations change in the blood.
Binding of oxygen to one haem group changes the conformation of the protein so the remaining haem groups bind oxygen more readily.
Haemoglobin molecules bind to one another once loaded, so oxygen is carried through the blood in molecular clusters.
mcqs.explain: Haemoglobin has four subunits, each with a haem group. When the first oxygen binds, the shape of the whole molecule shifts and the affinity of the other haem groups rises, so the second, third and fourth oxygen molecules bind progressively more easily. This is the basis of the S-shaped dissociation curve.
rationales: A student who pictures four separate sockets picks this. Independent binding would give a simple saturating curve; the haem groups interact through the protein, so binding at one raises the affinity of the rest.

A student who thinks carbon dioxide competes with oxygen at the haem groups picks this. Carbon dioxide binds allosterically, at sites on the polypeptide chains, and cooperative binding concerns oxygen alone.

Haemoglobin has four subunits, each with a haem group. When the first oxygen binds, the shape of the whole molecule shifts and the affinity of the other haem groups rises, so the second, third and fourth oxygen molecules bind progressively more easily. This is the basis of the S-shaped dissociation curve.
A student who reads 'cooperative' as cooperation between separate molecules picks this. The cooperation is within one molecule, between its four subunits; haemoglobin molecules do not join together.

mcqs.q: In the placenta, maternal blood and foetal blood are separated by a thin barrier. How is oxygen transferred from maternal blood to foetal blood?
options: Foetal haemoglobin has a lower affinity for oxygen, so that it releases oxygen to the rapidly growing foetal tissues more easily than adult haemoglobin would.
Maternal red blood cells pass across the barrier into the foetal circulation and deliver their oxygen directly to the foetus.
Maternal haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen rises in the placenta because the foetus needs oxygen, so it hands its oxygen on to the foetus.
Foetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen, so at the oxygen concentration in the placenta it loads oxygen that maternal haemoglobin releases.
mcqs.explain: Both haemoglobins experience the same oxygen concentration in the placenta. Maternal haemoglobin, with the lower affinity, unloads oxygen there; foetal haemoglobin, with its different subunits and higher affinity, binds that oxygen to a high saturation, so oxygen diffuses across the barrier into foetal blood.
rationales: A student who thinks about unloading rather than loading picks this. A lower affinity would prevent foetal haemoglobin taking oxygen from maternal blood in the first place; its affinity is higher, which is what allows the transfer.
A student who pictures the mother 'sharing her blood' picks this. The two circulations never mix; only dissolved substances such as oxygen diffuse across the placental barrier.

A student who equates affinity with delivery picks this. A rise in affinity would make maternal haemoglobin hold on to oxygen; transfer depends on maternal haemoglobin releasing oxygen and foetal haemoglobin, with the higher affinity, binding it.

Both haemoglobins experience the same oxygen concentration in the placenta. Maternal haemoglobin, with the lower affinity, unloads oxygen there; foetal haemoglobin, with its different subunits and higher affinity, binds that oxygen to a high saturation, so oxygen diffuses across the barrier into foetal blood.

mcqs.q: During vigorous exercise a muscle produces large amounts of carbon dioxide. How does this affect the delivery of oxygen to the muscle?
options: Carbon dioxide lowers haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so more oxygen dissociates at the oxygen concentration in the muscle.
Haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen rises in the working muscle so that it can hold on to more oxygen for delivery to the muscle cells.
Only the low oxygen concentration in the working muscle causes extra unloading; carbon dioxide itself has no effect on haemoglobin.
Carbon dioxide binds to the haem groups in place of oxygen, forcing the oxygen molecules off the haemoglobin.
mcqs.explain: This is the Bohr shift. Carbon dioxide binds allosterically to haemoglobin and lowers blood pH; both change the protein's conformation and reduce its affinity for oxygen. The dissociation curve shifts to the right, so a larger fraction of the oxygen carried is released in the tissue producing the most carbon dioxide.
rationales: This is the Bohr shift. Carbon dioxide binds allosterically to haemoglobin and lowers blood pH; both change the protein's conformation and reduce its affinity for oxygen. The dissociation curve shifts to the right, so a larger fraction of the oxygen carried is released in the tissue producing the most carbon dioxide.

A student who thinks greater need means greater affinity picks this. Higher affinity would keep oxygen bound to haemoglobin; the Bohr shift lowers the affinity so that more oxygen is released to the working muscle.

A student who applies only diffusion down a gradient picks this. Low oxygen concentration does promote unloading, but carbon dioxide additionally lowers haemoglobin's affinity, so at the same oxygen concentration more oxygen dissociates.

A student who generalizes from carbon monoxide picks this. Carbon dioxide does not bind at the haem groups; it binds allosterically to the polypeptide chains, which changes the protein's shape and lowers its affinity for oxygen.

mcqs.q: Adult haemoglobin is about 20% saturated with oxygen at a partial pressure of oxygen of 2 kPa, 60% at 4 kPa, 90% at 8 kPa and 98% at 13 kPa. Which explanation accounts for this pattern?
options: The four haem groups fill one after another at equal rates, so saturation rises in direct proportion to the oxygen concentration.
Saturation rises steeply from 2 to 8 kPa because each oxygen bound raises the affinity of the other haem groups.
The curve shows the order in which haemoglobin loads over time, from its arrival in the lungs to full saturation.
The plateau above 8 kPa is where haemoglobin releases most of its oxygen to tissues, because saturation is highest there.
mcqs.explain: At low oxygen concentration the first oxygen binds with difficulty, so saturation is low. Once bound, it changes the protein's conformation and the other haem groups bind more readily, giving the steep rise; above 8 kPa most haem groups are occupied and the curve levels off. This cooperative binding produces the S-shape.
rationales: A student who thinks the haem groups bind independently picks this. The data are not proportional: saturation triples between 2 and 4 kPa but rises only slightly between 8 and 13 kPa, which is the signature of cooperative binding followed by saturation.

At low oxygen concentration the first oxygen binds with difficulty, so saturation is low. Once bound, it changes the protein's conformation and the other haem groups bind more readily, giving the steep rise; above 8 kPa most haem groups are occupied and the curve levels off. This cooperative binding produces the S-shape.
A student who reads the x-axis as time picks this. The axis is oxygen concentration; each value gives the saturation haemoglobin reaches at that concentration, wherever and whenever it occurs.

A student who reads saturation as delivery picks this. The plateau corresponds to loading in the lungs; oxygen is released in the steep region, where a small fall in oxygen concentration causes a large fall in saturation.

mcqs.q: Two oxygen dissociation curves are compared. Curve X lies to the left of curve Y: at a partial pressure of oxygen of 4 kPa, haemoglobin X is 75% saturated and haemoglobin Y is 60% saturated. What can be concluded?
options: Haemoglobin X has the lower affinity for oxygen, because its curve lies further to the left on the axis.
Haemoglobin X loaded before Y, because the curve further to the left represents an earlier time.
Haemoglobin X has the higher affinity for oxygen, because it is more fully loaded at the same oxygen concentration as Y.
Haemoglobin X delivers more oxygen at 4 kPa, because a higher saturation means more oxygen is being released.
mcqs.explain: Affinity is compared at one oxygen concentration: X reaches a higher saturation than Y at 4 kPa, so it binds oxygen more readily. A curve further to the left always indicates higher affinity; foetal haemoglobin's curve lies to the left of the adult curve for this reason.
rationales: A student who reads 'left' as 'less' picks this. Comparing at the same concentration, X is more saturated than Y, so X holds oxygen more readily; a left-shifted curve means higher affinity.
A student who reads the x-axis as time picks this. The axis is oxygen concentration, so the two curves describe how each haemoglobin responds to concentration, not when each was loaded.

Affinity is compared at one oxygen concentration: X reaches a higher saturation than Y at 4 kPa, so it binds oxygen more readily. A curve further to the left always indicates higher affinity; foetal haemoglobin's curve lies to the left of the adult curve for this reason.
A student who confuses saturation with delivery picks this. Saturation is oxygen held, not oxygen given up; the higher affinity of X means it retains more oxygen at 4 kPa than Y does.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Lung adaptations are treated only for the alveolar lungs of a mammal: surfactant, the branched network of bronchioles, extensive capillary beds and high surface area. No content is included on bird lungs and air sacs, amphibian or reptile lungs, insect tracheal systems or cutaneous gas exchange; fish gills appear only where B3.1.3 names ventilation with water as a way of maintaining a concentration gradient.
